content: A vegetarian diet primarily excludes meat and fish and emphasizes plant-based foods including vegetables, fruits, grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds. Variants include lacto-vegetarianism (includes dairy), ovo-vegetarianism (includes eggs), and lacto-ovo vegetarianism (includes both dairy and eggs). Mechanistically, vegetarian diets tend to be higher in dietary fiber, antioxidants, and phytochemicals, while lower in saturated fat and cholesterol, contributing to benefits in cardiovascular and metabolic health. Well-planned vegetarian diets can provide adequate macronutrients and essential micronutrients but require attention to certain nutrients like vitamin B12, iron, calcium, omega-3 fatty acids, and protein diversity for completeness. The practical relevance lies in disease prevention, weight control, and environmental sustainability. Major synonyms and related terms include plant-based diet, meat-free diet, and vegan diet (which excludes all animal products). Limitations include potential risk of nutrient deficiencies if poorly planned and challenges for certain populations such as pregnant women or young children. Safety considerations are important to avoid unbalanced intake and to ensure adequate supplementation when needed. Overall, evidence supports that a balanced vegetarian diet is a healthy dietary pattern for all life stages when properly planned and executed.

chunk_title: Types of Vegetarian Diets and Definitions
content: Vegetarian diets vary by the inclusion or exclusion of animal-derived products. Lacto-vegetarians consume dairy but avoid eggs and meat; ovo-vegetarians include eggs but not dairy or meat; lacto-ovo vegetarians include both dairy and eggs. Vegan diets are a strict form of vegetarianism excluding all animal products. Understanding these distinctions is important when evaluating nutritional needs and health outcomes.
